newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FORECAST - UBS sees easier Swiss franc 97.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - UBS sees easier Swiss franc 97.

text.p: The Swiss franc should ease against the mark and dollar next year as low Swiss interest rates and slow growth keep the currency under pressure, Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) said in its latest economic outlook.
It warned that uncertainty surrounding the run-up to Europe's single currency could still drive funds into the franc, but added this was not the probable scenario.

Generous injections of money market liquidity by the Swiss National Bank (SNB), followed by a half-point discount rate cut on September 27, helped bring the franc off its recent highs by the end of the third quarter.

"Clearly better growth propsects for Germany compared with Switzerland should support this trend in the near future," UBS said. "But the risks that could arise on renewed turbulence on European currency markets should not be underestimated."

Autumn strikes by workers in France could weaken the government there and trigger a funds flow into Swiss francs, it added, but said markets' view of European economic and monetary union (EMU) would be the decisive factor for the currency next year.

"Should growth in Germany and France, pillars of European monetary union, pick up strongly and if it seems the Maastricht criteria will be fulfilled without accounting tricks, the mark should firm," it said.

"But if EMU is realised primarily via political considerations, without Germany and France fulfilling the Maastricht criteria, then huge capital transfers into the franc and a new appreciation would be the logical result. But this scenario still seems improbable. Despite an unstable dollar, we expect a slightly weaker franc against the mark."
If the franc continues to decline, money market rates could rise from recent lows below 1.5 percent, the bank said.

"In addition, the SNB could use reduced tension on foreign exchange markets to cautiously reduce excess liquidity. This could correct the recent rate slide on money markets to a level above 2 percent again from the middle of 1997."
On capital markets, yields traditionally have trouble staying below four percent, where they are now, UBS noted.

"This time, however, the long-term low inflation rate -- which has spurred fear of deflation in some market circles -- and the sideways interest rate trend in Europe could contribute to a longer phase of low yields," it said.
"For now we expect rates to stabilise just under 4 percent."

It added: "Because the spreads over short-term rates are large and real yields are relatively high, a moderate rise can be expected but only toward the end of 1997, when the economic recovery will gradually assume sharper focus."
UBS gave this outlook for Swiss franc exchange rates:
DEM USD GBP FRF ITL
